Calculate the corrected speed by dividing the rotational speed by the square root of a reference temperature of two hundred ninety eight kelvin. Determine the surge margin flow by multiplying the corrected speed by zero point zero zero one five and adding zero point five. Next, compute the actual corrected mass flow by dividing the mass flow by the square root of the reference temperature. Calculate the surge flow deviation by subtracting the surge margin flow from the actual corrected flow. Determine the surge pressure limit by multiplying the actual corrected flow by two point five and adding one point zero. Calculate the pressure deviation by subtracting the surge pressure limit from the pressure ratio. Calculate a safety metric by dividing the surge flow deviation by the surge margin flow and multiplying by one hundred. Return a list containing the corrected flow, pressure ratio, and the safety metric percentage. Example: given a flow of two, speed of ten thousand, and pressure of three hundred, return the computed operational states.

Evaluates whether a fiber optic link will operate reliably given the transmit power in decibel milliwatts, total fiber distance in kilometers, and the number of fusion splices. The entry function `budget(power, distance, splices)` defines the receiver sensitivity threshold as negative twenty eight decibel milliwatts. Calculate the total fiber attenuation by multiplying the distance by the standard loss of zero point two five decibels per kilometer. Calculate the total splice loss by multiplying the number of splices by zero point one decibels. Include a connector loss at both ends by adding zero point seven five decibels twice. Add a system repair margin of three decibels to account for future degradation. Compute the total system loss by summing the fiber attenuation, total splice loss, connector losses, and the repair margin. Determine the received optical power by subtracting the total system loss from the transmit power. Calculate the link power margin by subtracting the receiver sensitivity threshold from the received optical power. Check the link viability; assign a value of one if the power margin is greater than zero, otherwise assign zero. Return a list with the total system loss, the received optical power, the link power margin, and the viability indicator. Example: given a transmit power of zero, distance of forty, and four splices, return the power budget analysis.

Calculates the centrifugal tensile stress at the root of a gas turbine blade given the blade tip radius in meters, the rotational speed in revolutions per minute, and the root cross sectional area in square meters. The entry function `stress(radius, speed, area)` sets the material density to eight thousand kilograms per cubic meter. Define the hub radius as zero point four meters. Compute the angular velocity in radians per second by multiplying the rotational speed by pi, then dividing by thirty. Calculate the blade length by subtracting the hub radius from the tip radius. Determine the center of mass radius by adding half the blade length to the hub radius. Compute the total mass of the blade by multiplying the density by the root area and the blade length. In reality blades taper, so apply a taper reduction factor of zero point six to the total mass. Calculate the centrifugal force by multiplying the tapered mass by the center of mass radius and the square of the angular velocity. Find the root stress in pascals by dividing the centrifugal force by the root area. Convert the stress to megapascals by dividing by one million. Calculate the safety factor by dividing the material yield strength of eight hundred megapascals by the computed root stress. Return a list containing the angular velocity, the centrifugal force, the stress in megapascals, and the safety factor. Example: given a tip radius of zero point eight, speed of three thousand, and root area of zero point zero zero five, return the stress metrics.

Entry function `price(parameters)`. Input is a numeric vector of length five representing current asset price, strike price, risk free interest rate, volatility, and time to maturity in years. Calculate the intermediate mathematical terms for the standard pricing formula. Compute the normal cumulative distribution function values for these terms. Use these probabilities to calculate the final call option price and the put option price. Combine both final prices into a list. For example, given an input of one hundred, one hundred, zero point zero five, zero point two, and one, return a list with ten point four five and five point five seven.

Entry function `evaluate(bond)`. Input is a list containing face value, annual coupon rate, years to maturity, and current market price. Calculate the annual coupon payment amount. Use a discrete iterative approach to find the yield to maturity that equates the present value of all future cash flows to the market price. Calculate the present value of each cash flow using this yield. Determine the Macaulay duration by summing the time weighted present values and dividing by the market price. Return a numeric vector containing the calculated yield and the duration.

Entry function `update(results)`. Input is a numeric matrix where each row contains a player one rating, a player two rating, and a win indicator for player one. Iterate over each match row. Calculate the expected probability of winning for each player using the standard logistic rating curve formula. Calculate the rating change by multiplying a scaling factor of thirty two by the difference between the actual outcome and the expected outcome. Add the rating change to both players. Return a new matrix with the updated ratings for all matches.

Entry function `score(throws)`. Input is a list of plain text strings representing darts thrown in a single game of five hundred and one. The strings use words like twenty, double ten, or outer bull. Iterate over each throw and convert the text into its corresponding numerical value. Subtract this numerical value from the running total score. If a throw causes the remaining score to reach exactly one or drop below zero, mark that throw and all subsequent ones as invalid. Return a list containing the final remaining score and the count of valid throws.

Entry function `charge(sequence)`. Input is a single text string of uppercase amino acid letters. Split the string into individual characters. Count the total number of basic residues like lysine, arginine, and histidine. Count the acidic residues like aspartic acid and glutamic acid. Use standard acid dissociation constant formulas to calculate the partial charge of each group at a physiological baseline of seven point four. Sum the positive and negative contributions. Return the net numeric charge of the sequence.

Entry function `calculate(prices)`. Input is a numeric vector of consecutive daily closing prices. Iterate through the vector to compute the day to day price changes. Separate these changes into positive gains and absolute negative losses. Calculate the initial average gain and average loss over a rolling fourteen day period. Use a smoothed moving average for the subsequent days to update the average gains and losses. Compute the relative strength ratio and the final index value for each day. Return a numeric vector of the index.

Entry function `validate(grid)`. Input is a nine by nine numeric matrix representing a completed number puzzle. Check the matrix to ensure it contains only integers from one to nine. Iterate over every row and verify that it contains exactly nine unique numbers. Iterate over every column to verify the same condition. Divide the grid into nine separate three by three blocks and check each block for uniqueness. If any check fails, immediately store a false status. Return a single boolean indicating if all rules are satisfied.

Entry function `expand(temperatures)`. Input is a numeric vector of daily ambient temperatures in Celsius. Define a starting bridge length of one thousand meters and a standard thermal expansion coefficient. Iterate through the temperature readings. Calculate the temperature difference from a twenty degree baseline for each day. Calculate the linear expansion or contraction using the coefficient and the starting length. Update the daily length of the structure. Identify and store the maximum overall length and the maximum single day change. Return a list containing these two values.

Entry function `refract(angles)`. Input is a numeric vector of initial celestial observation angles in degrees. Iterate through each angle to apply a standard atmospheric refraction formula. Calculate a correction factor based on standard sea level temperature and pressure. Convert the initial degree angle into radians for trigonometric calculations. Compute the tangent of the angle and use it to find the refraction adjustment in arcminutes. Convert the adjustment back to degrees and subtract it from the initial angle. Return the numeric vector of true angles.

Entry function `estimate(grid)`. Input is a two dimensional numeric matrix consisting entirely of zeros and ones. Start with a block size equal to the matrix width. Count how many square blocks of this size contain at least one positive value. Divide the block size by two and repeat the counting process across the partitioned grid. Continue dividing and counting until the block size reaches a width of one. Calculate the natural logarithm of the sizes and the counts. Perform a linear regression and return the numeric slope of the line.

Entry function `build(text)`. Input is a plain text string. Split the string and count the frequency of each unique character. Create a list where each element represents a node with a character and its frequency. Start a loop that continues until only one node remains in the list. Inside the loop, identify the two nodes with the lowest frequencies. Create a new combined node whose frequency is the sum of the two. Remove the original two nodes and add the combined one back to the list. Return the final root frequency.

Entry function `mahalanobis(data)`. Input is a numeric matrix where rows represent samples and columns represent features. Calculate the arithmetic mean of each column. Create a new matrix by subtracting the respective column mean from every row. Calculate the covariance matrix by multiplying the transposed centered matrix by itself and dividing by the number of rows. Compute the mathematical inverse of this covariance matrix. For each row in the centered matrix, calculate the specific distance by multiplying the row by the inverse and then by the transposed row. Return the numeric distances.

Implement a function `merge_lists` that takes two lists (vectors) as input and returns a new list containing all elements from both input lists. For example, `merge_lists(c(1, 2), c(3, 4))` should return `c(1, 2, 3, 4)`, and `merge_lists(list('a', 'b'), list('c'))` should return `list('a', 'b', 'c')`.

Write a function `simple_interest` that calculates the simple interest given principal, rate, and time. The function should take `principal`, `rate` (as a decimal), and `time` (in years) as inputs and return the calculated simple interest. For example, `simple_interest(1000, 0.05, 2)` should return `100`, and `simple_interest(5000, 0.03, 1)` should return `150`.

topic: Find Common Elements in Two Vectors
text_es: Write a function `common_elements` that takes two vectors as input and returns a new vector containing only the elements that are common to both input vectors. For example, `common_elements(c(1, 2, 3), c(2, 3, 4))` should return `c(2, 3)`, and `common_elements(c('a', 'b'), c('c', 'd'))` should return `character(0)`.

Implement a function `filter_vector` that takes a numeric vector and a threshold value as input. It should return a new vector containing only the elements from the input vector that are greater than the threshold. For example, `filter_vector(c(10, 5, 20, 8), 10)` should return `c(20)`, and `filter_vector(c(1, 2, 3), 5)` should return `numeric(0)`.

Write a script `get_current_date` that returns the current date in 'YYYY-MM-DD' format. The script should not take any arguments. For example, `get_current_date()` should return a string like `'2023-10-27'` (depending on the actual date).

Create a function `file_exists_check` that takes a file path (string) as input and returns `TRUE` if the file exists at that path, and `FALSE` otherwise. For example, if 'temp.txt' exists, `file_exists_check('temp.txt')` should return `TRUE`. If 'nonexistent.txt' does not exist, `file_exists_check('nonexistent.txt')` should return `FALSE`.

Write a function `coin_flip` that simulates a single coin flip. It should take no arguments and return either `'Heads'` or `'Tails'` with equal probability. For example, `coin_flip()` could return `'Heads'`, and another call `coin_flip()` could return `'Tails'`.

Write a function `get_keys` that takes a named vector (acting as a dictionary) as input and returns a character vector of its names (keys). For example, `get_keys(c(name='Alice', age=30))` should return `c('name', 'age')`, and `get_keys(c(city='NY'))` should return `c('city')`.

Implement a function `simple_search` that takes a character vector (lines of text) and a `query` string as input. It should return a logical vector indicating which lines contain the query string (case-insensitive). For example, `simple_search(c('apple', 'Banana', 'Orange'), 'a')` should return `c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)`, and `simple_search(c('hello', 'world'), 'xyz')` should return `c(FALSE, FALSE)`.

Write a function `round_to_integer` that takes a numeric vector as input and returns a new vector with all numbers rounded to the nearest integer. For example, `round_to_integer(c(2.3, 2.7, 2.5))` should return `c(2, 3, 2)`, and `round_to_integer(c(-1.2, -1.8))` should return `c(-1, -2)`.

Create a function `roll_dice` that simulates rolling a standard six-sided die. It should take no arguments and return an integer between 1 and 6. For example, `roll_dice()` could return `3`, and another call `roll_dice()` could return `6`.

Implement a function `replace_substring` that takes a `main_string`, a `target_substring`, and a `replacement_substring` as input. It should return the `main_string` with all occurrences of `target_substring` replaced by `replacement_substring`. For example, `replace_substring('hello world', 'world', 'there')` should return `'hello there'`, and `replace_substring('banana', 'a', 'o')` should return `'bonono'`.

Write a function `schedule_task` that takes a `task_name` (string) and a `time` (string in 'HH:MM' format) as input. It should print a message indicating the task is scheduled. This is a conceptual task; no actual scheduling mechanism is required. For example, `schedule_task('Meeting', '10:30')` should print `'Task 'Meeting' scheduled for 10:30.'`, and `schedule_task('Lunch', '12:00')` should print `'Task 'Lunch' scheduled for 12:00.'`.

topic: Check if All Elements are Unique
text_es: Create a function `all_unique` that takes a vector as input and returns `TRUE` if all elements in the vector are unique, and `FALSE` otherwise. For example, `all_unique(c(1, 2, 3))` should return `TRUE`, and `all_unique(c(1, 2, 2))` should return `FALSE`.

Write a function `nth_smallest` that takes a numeric vector and an integer `n` as input. It should return the `n`-th smallest element in the vector. Assume `n` is always valid (i.e., `1 <= n <= length(vector)`). For example, `nth_smallest(c(5, 2, 8, 1), 2)` should return `2`, and `nth_smallest(c(10, 3, 7), 1)` should return `3`.

Implement a function `count_frequency` that takes a vector as input and returns a named integer vector where names are the unique elements and values are their frequencies. For example, `count_frequency(c('a', 'b', 'a', 'c'))` should return `c(a = 2, b = 1, c = 1)`, and `count_frequency(c(1, 2, 1, 3, 2))` should return `c('1' = 2, '2' = 2, '3' = 1)`.

Implement a function `days_between` that takes two date strings in 'YYYY-MM-DD' format as input and returns the number of days between them. The order of dates doesn't matter; the result should be positive. For example, `days_between('2023-01-01', '2023-01-05')` should return `4`, and `days_between('2023-01-05', '2023-01-01')` should return `4`.

Implement a function `categorize_numbers` that takes a numeric vector as input and returns a character vector where each element is categorized as 'Positive', 'Negative', or 'Zero'. For example, `categorize_numbers(c(1, -2, 0, 5))` should return `c('Positive', 'Negative', 'Zero', 'Positive')`, and `categorize_numbers(c(-10))` should return `c('Negative')`.

topic: Filter Data Frame Rows by Column Value
text_es: Write a function `filter_dataframe` that takes a data frame, a `column_name` (string), and a `value` as input. It should return a new data frame containing only the rows where the specified column's value matches the given `value`. For example, `df <- data.frame(name = c('A', 'B', 'C'), score = c(10, 20, 10)); filter_dataframe(df, 'score', 10)` should return rows for 'A' and 'C'.

Create a function `string_permutations` that takes a short string (e.g., up to 3 characters) and returns a character vector of all unique permutations of its characters. For example, `string_permutations('ab')` should return `c('ab', 'ba')`, and `string_permutations('abc')` should return `c('abc', 'acb', 'bac', 'bca', 'cab', 'cba')`.

Implement a function `reverse_words(sentence)` that takes a string representing a sentence and returns a new string where the order of words is reversed. Words are separated by single spaces. The input will not have leading/trailing spaces. For example: `reverse_words("hello world")` should return `"world hello"`. `reverse_words("one two three")` should return `"three two one"`.

Implement a function `rectangle_perimeter(length, width)` that calculates the perimeter of a rectangle given its length and width. Both inputs are positive numbers. For example: `rectangle_perimeter(4, 5)` should return `18`. `rectangle_perimeter(2.5, 3)` should return `11`.

Write a function `concatenate_vectors(vec1, vec2)` that takes two vectors of the same type and returns a new vector containing all elements from both. For example: `concatenate_vectors(c(1, 2), c(3, 4))` should return `c(1, 2, 3, 4)`. `concatenate_vectors(c("a", "b"), c("c"))` should return `c("a", "b", "c")`.

Create a function `compound_interest(principal, rate, time, n)` that calculates the final amount after compound interest. `principal` is the initial amount, `rate` is the annual interest rate (as a decimal), `time` is the number of years, and `n` is the number of times interest is compounded per year. For example: `compound_interest(1000, 0.05, 1, 1)` should return `1050`. `compound_interest(1000, 0.04, 2, 4)` should return approximately `1082.8567`.

Implement a function `remove_element(vec, element)` that takes a vector and an element, and returns a new vector with all occurrences of the specified element removed. For example: `remove_element(c(1, 2, 3, 2), 2)` should return `c(1, 3)`. `remove_element(c("apple", "banana", "cherry"), "banana")` should return `c("apple", "cherry")`.

Create a function `arithmetic_sequence(start, diff, count)` that generates a numeric vector representing an arithmetic sequence. `start` is the first term, `diff` is the common difference, and `count` is the number of terms. For example: `arithmetic_sequence(1, 2, 5)` should return `c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9)`. `arithmetic_sequence(10, -1, 3)` should return `c(10, 9, 8)`.

Create a function `get_named_vector_values(nv)` that takes a named vector and returns a simple (unnamed) vector containing only its values. For example: `get_named_vector_values(c(a=10, b=20))` should return `c(10, 20)`. `get_named_vector_values(c(fruit="apple", color="red"))` should return `c("apple", "red")`.

Implement a function `is_weekend(date_str)` that takes a date string in 'YYYY-MM-DD' format and returns `TRUE` if it's a Saturday or Sunday, and `FALSE` otherwise. For example: `is_weekend("2023-10-28")` should return `TRUE` (Saturday). `is_weekend("2023-10-27")` should return `FALSE` (Friday).

Implement a function `parse_csv_numbers(csv_str)` that takes a string of comma-separated numbers and returns a numeric vector. For example: `parse_csv_numbers("1,2,3.5")` should return `c(1, 2, 3.5)`. `parse_csv_numbers("100")` should return `c(100)`.

Write a function `generate_alphanumeric_string(length)` that generates a random string of specified `length` containing uppercase letters (A-Z) and digits (0-9). For example: `generate_alphanumeric_string(5)` might return `"A1B3C"`. `generate_alphanumeric_string(10)` might return `"X8L0P2Q7R5"`.

Create a function `check_inventory(inventory, product_name)` that takes a named vector `inventory` (product names as names, quantities as values) and a `product_name`. It returns the quantity of the product or 0 if not found. For example: `check_inventory(c(apple=10, banana=5), "apple")` should return `10`. `check_inventory(c(apple=10), "orange")` should return `0`.

topic: Filter Data Frame Columns by Type
text_es: Implement a function `filter_df_by_type(df, type_name)` that takes a data frame `df` and a string `type_name` (e.g., 'numeric', 'character'). It returns a new data frame containing only columns of the specified type. For example: `df <- data.frame(a=1, b="x", c=TRUE); filter_df_by_type(df, "numeric")` should return a data frame with just column `a`. `filter_df_by_type(df, "character")` should return a data frame with just column `b`.

Implement a function `get_keys_by_value(nv, target_value)` that takes a named vector `nv` and a `target_value`. It returns a character vector of names (keys) whose corresponding values match `target_value`. For example: `get_keys_by_value(c(a=1, b=2, c=1), 1)` should return `c("a", "c")`. `get_keys_by_value(c(x="red", y="blue"), "green")` should return `character(0)`.

Write a function `simulate_card_draw(deck, num_cards)` that simulates drawing `num_cards` from a `deck` (character vector of cards, e.g., '2H', 'AD'). It returns a character vector of the drawn cards without replacement. Assume `num_cards` is less than or equal to `length(deck)`. For example: `deck <- c("AH", "KD", "5C"); simulate_card_draw(deck, 2)` might return `c("KD", "AH")` (order can vary). `simulate_card_draw(c("A", "B", "C"), 1)` might return `c("B")`.

Write a function `weighted_average(values, weights)` that calculates the weighted average of a numeric vector `values` given a corresponding numeric vector `weights`. Both vectors must have the same length. For example: `weighted_average(c(10, 20, 30), c(1, 2, 3))` should return `23.33333`. `weighted_average(c(5, 10), c(0.5, 0.5))` should return `7.5`.

topic: Filter Data Frame by Multiple Conditions
text_es: Implement a function `filter_df_multi_cond(df, col1_name, col1_val, col2_name, col2_val)` that filters a data frame `df` based on two conditions: `col1_name` equals `col1_val` AND `col2_name` equals `col2_val`. Return the filtered data frame. For example: `df <- data.frame(id=1:3, type=c("A", "B", "A"), value=c(10, 20, 10)); filter_df_multi_cond(df, "type", "A", "value", 10)` should return a data frame with rows 1 and 3.

Create a function `summarize_vector(vec)` that takes a numeric vector and returns a named vector containing its 'min', 'max', 'mean', and 'median' values. For example: `summarize_vector(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))` should return `c(min=1, max=5, mean=3, median=3)`. `summarize_vector(c(10, 20, 0, 5))` should return `c(min=0, max=20, mean=8.75, median=7.5)`.

Create a function `generate_random_letters(count, uppercase = TRUE)` that generates a character vector of `count` random letters. If `uppercase` is `TRUE`, generate uppercase letters; otherwise, lowercase. For example: `generate_random_letters(3)` might return `c("F", "P", "X")`. `generate_random_letters(2, uppercase = FALSE)` might return `c("g", "a")`.

Create a function `hamming_distance` that computes the Hamming distance between two strings of equal length. The Hamming distance is the number of positions at which the corresponding symbols are different. 

Example 1: `hamming_distance("karolin", "kathrin")` should return `3`.
Example 2: `hamming_distance("abc", "abd")` should return `1`.

Write a function `decimal_to_binary` that takes a non-negative integer (base-10) and returns its binary string representation. 

Example 1: `decimal_to_binary(13)` should return `"1101"`.
Example 2: `decimal_to_binary(0)` should return `"0"`.

Implement a function `is_balanced_parentheses` that determines if the parentheses in a given string are balanced. Only consider '(', ')', '[', ']', '{', '}'.

Example 1: `is_balanced_parentheses("{[()]}")` should return `TRUE`.
Example 2: `is_balanced_parentheses("([)]")` should return `FALSE`.

Write a function `calculate_dot_product` that computes the dot product of two numeric vectors. Assume both input vectors are of the same length.

Example 1: `calculate_dot_product(c(1, 2, 3), c(4, 5, 6))` should return `32` (1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6).
Example 2: `calculate_dot_product(c(1, 0), c(0, 1))` should return `0`.

Implement a function `find_second_smallest` that takes a numeric vector and returns its second smallest unique element. Assume the vector contains at least two unique elements.

Example 1: `find_second_smallest(c(5, 2, 8, 2, 1))` should return `2`.
Example 2: `find_second_smallest(c(10, 20, 30))` should return `20`.

Write a function `simple_moving_average` that calculates the simple moving average for a given numeric vector and a window size. The result should be a vector of the same length, with `NA` for periods where an average cannot be computed.

Example 1: `simple_moving_average(c(10, 12, 14, 16, 18), 3)` should return `c(NA, NA, 12, 14, 16)`.
Example 2: `simple_moving_average(c(1, 2, 3, 4), 2)` should return `c(NA, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5)`.

Create a function `categorize_ages` that takes a numeric vector of ages and returns a factor vector categorizing them into 'Child' (0-12), 'Teen' (13-19), 'Adult' (20-64), and 'Senior' (65+). 

Example 1: `categorize_ages(c(7, 15, 30, 70))` should return `factor(c("Child", "Teen", "Adult", "Senior"))`.
Example 2: `categorize_ages(c(19, 65))` should return `factor(c("Teen", "Senior"))`.

Write a function `unique_elements_in_order` that takes a vector and returns a new vector containing only the unique elements, preserving their first-occurrence order. 

Example 1: `unique_elements_in_order(c(1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4))` should return `c(1, 2, 3, 4)`.
Example 2: `unique_elements_in_order(c('a', 'b', 'c', 'a', 'b'))` should return `c('a', 'b', 'c')`.

Create a function `euclidean_distance_nd` that calculates the Euclidean distance between two numeric vectors (points) of arbitrary but equal dimension. 

Example 1: `euclidean_distance_nd(c(1, 1), c(4, 5))` should return `5`.
Example 2: `euclidean_distance_nd(c(0, 0, 0), c(1, 1, 1))` should return `sqrt(3)`.

Implement a function `extract_digits` that takes a string and returns a vector of all digits found in it, in their original order. 

Example 1: `extract_digits("abc123def45")` should return `c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)`.
Example 2: `extract_digits("no numbers here")` should return `numeric(0)`.

topic: Calculate Mean of Named Vector Values
text_es:
Write a function `mean_named_vector_values` that takes a named numeric vector and returns the mean of its values. 

Example 1: `mean_named_vector_values(c(a=10, b=20, c=30))` should return `20`.
Example 2: `mean_named_vector_values(c(x=5))` should return `5`.

topic: Filter Data Frame by Multiple Columns
text_es:
Implement a function `filter_df_by_conditions` that takes a data frame, a column name, a value, another column name, and another value. It should return a data frame containing only rows where the first column equals the first value AND the second column equals the second value. 

Example 1: `df <- data.frame(A=c(1,2,3), B=c('x','y','x')); filter_df_by_conditions(df, 'A', 1, 'B', 'x')` should return `data.frame(A=1, B='x')`.
Example 2: `df <- data.frame(ID=c(1,2), Status=c('Active','Inactive')); filter_df_by_conditions(df, 'ID', 2, 'Status', 'Active')` should return an empty data frame.

topic: Remove Duplicates from List of Lists
text_es:
Create a function `remove_duplicate_sublists` that takes a list of numeric vectors (sublists) and returns a new list with duplicate sublists removed. The order of unique sublists should be preserved.

Example 1: `remove_duplicate_sublists(list(c(1,2), c(3,4), c(1,2)))` should return `list(c(1,2), c(3,4))`.
Example 2: `remove_duplicate_sublists(list(c(1), c(2), c(1)))` should return `list(c(1), c(2))`.

topic: Check if All Elements are Greater Than Value
text_es:
Write a function `all_greater_than` that takes a numeric vector and a single numeric value, and returns `TRUE` if all elements in the vector are strictly greater than the value, otherwise `FALSE`.

Example 1: `all_greater_than(c(5, 6, 7), 4)` should return `TRUE`.
Example 2: `all_greater_than(c(5, 6, 7), 7)` should return `FALSE`.

Implement a function `cylinder_volume` that calculates the volume of a cylinder given its radius and height. Use `pi` from R's constants.

Example 1: `cylinder_volume(radius = 2, height = 3)` should return `37.69911` (approx).
Example 2: `cylinder_volume(radius = 1, height = 1)` should return `3.141593` (approx).

Create a function `sort_named_vector_by_value` that takes a named numeric vector and returns a new named vector sorted in ascending order of its values. 

Example 1: `sort_named_vector_by_value(c(b=20, a=10, c=30))` should return `c(a=10, b=20, c=30)`.

  sorted_names <- vector_names[order_indices]

is_sorted_ascending <- function(vec) {
  len_vec <- length(vec)
  if (len_vec <= 1) {
    return(TRUE)
  }

  is_ascending <- TRUE
  for (i in 1:(len_vec - 1)) {
    current_val <- vec[i]
    next_val <- vec[i+1]
    if (current_val >= next_val) {
      is_ascending <- FALSE
      break
    }
  }
  return(is_ascending)
}

Example: `extract_domain('https://www.example.com/path/to/page')` should return `'example.com'`. `extract_domain('http://sub.domain.org')` should return `'sub.domain.org'`.

extract_domain <- function(url_string) {
  # Remove protocol (http://, https://)
  protocol_pattern <- "^(http|https)://(www\\.)?"
  cleaned_url <- sub(protocol_pattern, "", url_string)

  # Remove anything after the first '/'
  path_start <- gregexpr("/", cleaned_url, fixed = TRUE)[[1]][1]
  if (path_start > 0) {
    domain_with_port <- substr(cleaned_url, 1, path_start - 1)
  } else {
    domain_with_port <- cleaned_url
  }

  # Remove port number if present
  port_pattern <- ":[0-9]{1,5}$"
  final_domain <- sub(port_pattern, "", domain_with_port)

  # Remove www. prefix if still present (edge case for some URLs without protocol)
  www_prefix <- "^www\\."
  domain_no_www <- sub(www_prefix, "", final_domain)

  return(domain_no_www)
}

calculate_age <- function(birthdate, current_date = Sys.Date()) {
  birth_year <- as.numeric(format(birthdate, "%Y"))
  current_year <- as.numeric(format(current_date, "%Y"))

  age <- current_year - birth_year

  birth_month_day <- format(birthdate, "%m-%d")
  current_month_day <- format(current_date, "%m-%d")

  is_birthday_past <- birth_month_day <= current_month_day

  if (!is_birthday_past) {
    age <- age - 1
  }

  return(age)
}
